name: Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
what: This subtopic covers synaptic plasticity as the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience, including the three mechanisms — sprouting, rerouting, and pruning — and the two forms of plasticity underlying learning and memory: long-term potentiation and long-term depression.
why: Synaptic plasticity is the neurological explanation for how learning and memory occur. It connects directly to the neurotransmitter content from lesson 2C — particularly glutamate's role — and is assessed through both recall and complex application questions involving realistic learning scenarios.

items.title: I can define synaptic plasticity and explain its relationship to learning and memory
items.what: Synaptic plasticity is the ability of synaptic connections to change over time in response to activity or experience. It is the fundamental mechanism of memory formation that leads to learning. When experiences cause neurons to coactivate, their synaptic connections physically change, forming memory traces — neural pathways that represent what has been learnt.
items.why: This definition is precise and must be stated accurately in exam responses. A common error is defining synaptic plasticity as the ability of the brain (rather than synaptic connections specifically) to change — this wording loses marks.
items.example: A student practising multiplication tables each day causes the neurons involved in that knowledge to coactivate repeatedly. Their synaptic connections strengthen over time, forming a memory trace that makes recall faster and more reliable.

items.title: I can explain sprouting as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity
items.what: Sprouting is the ability of dendrites or axons to develop new extensions or branches. This increases the reach of the neuron and enables the formation of new synaptic connections with other neurons.
items.why: Sprouting is the structural mechanism behind the formation of new synaptic connections during learning and recovery from brain injury. It appears as one of the structural changes listed under long-term potentiation in exam responses.
items.example: When a person learns a new skill such as knitting, sprouting in the relevant brain regions allows dendritic branches to extend and form new connections with neighbouring neurons, expanding the neural pathway associated with that skill.

items.title: I can explain rerouting as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity
items.what: Rerouting is the ability of a neuron connected to a damaged neuron to abandon that connection and form a new synaptic connection with an undamaged neuron instead. This reestablishes the synaptic connection via an alternative route, restoring brain functioning.
items.why: Rerouting explains how the brain can partially recover function after injury by finding alternative neural pathways. It is distinct from sprouting (which forms entirely new connections) and pruning (which removes connections).
items.example: After a stroke damages neurons in a motor pathway, rerouting may allow neighbouring undamaged neurons to form alternative connections that partially restore the ability to move the affected limb over weeks of rehabilitation.

items.title: I can explain pruning as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity
items.what: Pruning is the elimination of synaptic connections that are not adequately activated. When synaptic connections are not used, they are removed to accommodate stronger and more essential connections, enhancing the efficiency of brain functioning.
items.why: Students frequently assume pruning is harmful because it removes connections. The correct understanding is that pruning is adaptive — it frees neural resources for connections that are used more frequently, improving overall brain efficiency.
items.example: A person who learnt to play the recorder in primary school but has not played for 15 years will find that those synaptic connections have been pruned, making the skill harder to perform. The brain allocated those resources to more frequently used pathways.

items.title: I can explain long-term potentiation, including the structural changes it produces at the neural synapse
items.what: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is the long-lasting, experience-dependent strengthening of synaptic connections that are regularly coactivated. Repeated high-intensity stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron — driven by increased glutamate release — produces three structural changes: an increased number of receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron's dendrites, bushier dendrites due to sprouting, and an increased number of synaptic connections due to sprouting.
items.why: LTP is the neurological mechanism of learning — it explains why practice makes performance faster and more efficient. Exam questions require students to name and describe the specific structural changes, not just state that connections strengthen.
items.example: A person learning to type using a new keyboard layout practises daily for two months. LTP in the relevant neural pathways increases the number of receptor sites and produces bushier dendrites, making the pathway more efficient and typing progressively faster and more accurate.

items.title: I can explain long-term depression, including the structural changes it produces at the neural synapse
items.what: Long-term depression (LTD) is the long-lasting, experience-dependent weakening of synaptic connections between neurons that are not regularly coactivated. Infrequent, low-intensity stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron produces three structural changes: a decreased number of receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron's dendrites, fewer dendrites due to pruning, and a decreased number of synaptic connections due to pruning.
items.why: LTD is adaptive — it prevents the brain from maintaining unnecessary connections and frees resources for more relevant memory traces. It also explains forgetting and skill loss after periods of disuse.
items.example: A student who studied Indonesian in Year 8 but stopped practising for five years experiences LTD in the relevant neural pathways: receptor sites are reduced, dendrites are pruned, and the connections weaken — making Indonesian vocabulary increasingly difficult to recall.

items.title: I can compare long-term potentiation and long-term depression, identifying one similarity and one difference
items.what: Similarity: both LTP and LTD are long-lasting, experience-dependent forms of synaptic plasticity that involve structural changes to the neural synapse. Difference: LTP results from frequent coactivation and strengthens synaptic connections (involving sprouting), whereas LTD results from infrequent coactivation and weakens synaptic connections (involving pruning).
items.why: Comparing LTP and LTD is a standard exam question type. Students must use the precise terms 'strengthening' and 'weakening' rather than informal language, and must link each process to the correct mechanism.
items.example: A musician who practises daily experiences LTP in the relevant motor pathways (connections strengthen via sprouting). If they stop practising for a year, LTD weakens those same connections via pruning. Resuming practice can restrengthen the connections through LTP again.

items.title: I can apply long-term potentiation and long-term depression to a novel learning scenario
items.what: LTP occurs when a person regularly practises or uses a skill or knowledge, causing the relevant synaptic connections to strengthen and the neural pathway to become more efficient. LTD occurs when a previously learned skill or knowledge is no longer regularly used, causing those synaptic connections to weaken and become less efficient.
items.why: VCE exam questions routinely present a new scenario — such as a person learning a sport, instrument, or work skill — and ask students to explain the role of LTP and/or LTD. Applying the concepts to an unfamiliar context is the highest-level skill tested.
items.example: Duncan's employees learn a new typing method over two months (LTP: the neural pathways for the new method are repeatedly coactivated, strengthening those connections). Simultaneously, LTD weakens the old typing method's neural pathway because it is no longer being regularly used, helping employees abandon the old habit.
